abstract:
Research on B cells in central nervous system (CNS) diseases rests on a mature multiple sclerosis (MS) literature, whereas evidence in CNS injury and neurodegeneration is still emerging. We mapped publications from 2006 to 2026 and separated bibliometric visibility from mechanistic maturity.
We searched the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) on August 17, 2026, for English-language records carrying the Article document-type tag and published from January 1, 2006, through August 17, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened all records, with unresolved disagreements adjudicated by a third reviewer. Publication trends, collaboration, co-citation, journal flows, citation bursts, and keyword evolution were analyzed using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, bibliometrix, R, and SCImago Graphica. Search materials, parameters, and source tables were archived.
After database-level limits, 2,701 records were screened; 467 (17.3%) were excluded and 2,234 (82.7%) included. The corpus had accrued 91,218 WoSCC citations. Annual output rose from 91 articles in 2016 to 231 in 2025; 173 articles from 2026 represent a partial year. The United States contributed the most articles, and the University of California, San Francisco ranked first after affiliation normalization. Co-citation and keyword analyses showed an MS/experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE)-centered foundation built around B-cell depletion trials, meningeal pathology, diagnostic criteria, and regulatory B-cell biology. Recent bursts included anti-CD20 therapy, single-cell RNA sequencing, autoimmune encephalitis, ischemic stroke, Mendelian randomization, B-cell depletion, and Alzheimer disease.
B-cell-related CNS research has expanded, but evidence maturity remains disease-specific. MS/EAE provides the clearest foundation. Findings in CNS injury, neurodegeneration, and candidate peripheral-CNS routes remain context-dependent and require validation by disease, anatomical compartment, B-cell state, and stage. Bibliometric prominence reveals attention, not shared causality or therapeutic efficacy.

New ZealandJ Inflamm Res1015126841178-7031B cells are well established as important contributors to multiple sclerosis, but their roles in other brain and spinal cord disorders are less clear. We examined 2,234 research articles published between 2006 and August 2026 to see how the field developed, who worked together, which papers shaped it, and which topics are gaining attention. The literature remains centered on multiple sclerosis and its experimental models, especially studies of B-cell-depleting treatments and B-cell accumulation around the meninges. Research is expanding into autoimmune encephalitis, stroke, neurodegeneration, and communication between peripheral organs and the central nervous system, but much of this work is still disease-specific or based on animal models. We therefore separated highly visible topics from mechanisms supported by stronger human evidence. We also archived the search strategy, screening codebook, scripts, and source data so the analysis can be checked. The main message is that B cells should not be treated as one uniform target across all central nervous system diseases: the relevant B-cell state, location, disease stage, and biological function need to be defined before findings can guide treatment.© 2026 Li et al.B cellsbibliometric analysiscentral nervous systemmultiple sclerosisneuroinflammationscience mappingWen-Jing Zhong reports support for the work from National Natural Science Foundation of China, during the conduct of the study.
